en: The *Śikṣā* of Pārāśarya is the *Pārāśarīśikṣā*;
now I shall proclaim the *Śikṣā* according to the doctrine of Pārāśara.
Just as Viśvātman is among the gods, and as Puṣkara is among sacred fords,
so is the instruction of Parāśara proclaimed in all the scriptures.
Now I shall explain the Praṇava, which has three morae and three deities.
That which possesses three forms, three colors, three locations, and likewise three qualities,
consisting of eighty-one syllables, is remembered as the first *kaṇḍikā*.
According to the methods described in the *lakṣaṇa*, "iṣe tvā" is the illustrative example.
Three, three, four, ten, five, and the eighth is recorded;
likewise, the eleventh syllable is seen in both.
Furthermore, the seventh and the fifth are indeed the eleventh syllable again. 4–5.
One should know that there are nine syllables [in the first half-verse] and eleven syllables in the statement;
six end at the final pause, while these five consist of three half-verses.
One should know that the fourth [line] consists of one [syllable], and the remaining are recorded as having pairs of half-verses.
There is nothing higher than high, nor likewise anything lower than low.
Thus the vowels (varṇas) are to be employed; "iṣe tvā" is the illustration.
Seven, three, and four are proclaimed as the eight vowels (vasu-varṇas). 7–8.
Six, two, and eight are attained; this is remembered as the second section (kaṇḍikā).
The first indeed has the number of Rudras (eleven), the second has the number seven, the third should have the number of treasures (nine), and the fourth has the number of Vasus (eight).
The fifth is the number of Vedas (four), and the third is known as the Kaṇḍikā (ten). Likewise, the first statement is eight, the second is five, the third is forty, then seven, forty, and nine.
The measure of syllables in the *Vasordhārā* is optionally thirty-four or ninety-nine syllables;
thus the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*) has been declared— so said the sage Pārāśara.

The seventh, the ninth, and likewise the eighth—these are the phonemes that should be employed. *Vītihotra* is the illustration for both; in the middle of both *kaṇḍikās*, the labial sound (*uṣṭhya*) is never found. 14.
Agni and Yajus consist of three and a half [verses] and four [syllables];
there are ten syllables and five [verses], with Agni as the illustration of light.
There are seven syllables and four [verses], which is remembered as Yamadagni.
Ten syllables, four [times], ten syllables, twelve syllables;
at the end, a pair of syllables is the statement for the sake of intention and as an illustration.
Nine syllables, three, and indeed three, and six syllables. 16–17.
Such sentences exist; there is the example "sim̐hyasi," as well as "yam paridhim atra pitaraḥ" and "ayaṃ te ca iḍe.
Likewise, there are five sections beginning with "yo devebhyaḥ," even without the letter *sakāra*.
The twenty-four syllables beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ha' are declared to be like the Gāyatrī— purifying and situated in the midst of sacrifice.
[The verses] "Agnim īḷe dūtam" and "Vasantāya kapiñjalān" are for Prajāpati, and there are two pairs.
The first [vartikā] ends with a sibilant (ūṣman), while the remaining ones end with vowels;
the second is the pure one, presided over by the first [vowel], and the third is the "pressing" one, presided over by the second.
The first should be known as *cidasi*, and then it should follow from the *armma*s. 21.
The two *kaṇḍikās* concerning both *dhyakṣa* and *dhyakṣānta* are correctly [explained] as follows: 22.
Where there is a solitary *va* (*vakāra*), a *ra* (*repha*) is also situated below it, and a dental [consonant] is to be known as being above; "yūpavraska" is the illustrative example. 23.

One should recognize that there is neither an anusvāra, nor a conjunct consonant, nor a visarga, nor even lengthening; for that which follows the letter *e* is to be known as it stands alone. With a mora (*mātrā*) it becomes long, and without a mora it is short.
One should understand these syllables thus: "quick" (kṣipram) becomes "long" (dīrgham).
"Quick" and "long" are explained as being one finger-breadth apart;
"quick" would be half of "long. There is no "lengthiness" in "quick. 25–26.

Just as the duration of a long vowel is proclaimed, so too is that of a sibilant (ūṣman); a sibilant makes a long vowel equal in length to half of it. If a conjunct consonant is seen following an anusvāra, [the same applies].
One should recognize shortness as the portion belonging to the *saṃsrava*; this is the illustration.
(28) When a closed [vowel] is seen there above an *anusvāra*, one should recognize that as long; "the listener is a pressing-stone" is the illustration. (29)
If an *anusvāra* follows a long vowel,
it is declared to be short by way of an option (*vibhāṣā*) specifically in mantras; however,
in the case of consonants and so forth, the *anusvāra* consists of two morae (*dvimātra*).

One should know that [syllable] to be long, according to the illustration "from the hearts of the gods. Furthermore, if a conjunct consonant is seen following an *anusvāra*, one should know that [syllable] to be short, both in the mantras and in the Brāhmaṇas.
From a short vowel at the beginning, a long one arises; from a long vowel at the beginning, a light one arises.
A non-long vowel attains length, yet there is no inherent length in that which is already long.
There is no short vowel following a conjunct consonant or similar [obstructive]; such is the length of the long vowel.
Wherever a consonant cluster (saṃyoga) or similar [feature] follows, there the vowel is certainly short; they know it to be *abhinīta*, *nipāta*, *jātya*, or *svarita*.
This occurs precisely at the time of the sentence (*vākya*), according to the sequence at the time of recitation (*pāṭha*).
The measure for the *jātya* and *anupatha* types of hand is six finger-breadths;

it should be exactly one-fourth of that [for the *pūrṇa* type], and one should further fashion the *nipāta*, the *abhinīta*, and the remaining *nīcatara* types in gradual succession according to that same proportion. (36–37)
One should recognize that as having three accents; "with clarified butter" is the illustration.
One should employ [the vowels] in a low tone, even lower, and again low;
such is the manner in which the phonemes (varṇas) are to be employed—this is the illustration for "vigor" (ojas).
These sounds—ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, and m—are nasalized (anunāsika).
They occur as *pratyayas* when they are joined with the semivowels (*antasthā*), as well as with the letter *ha*, and with the third and fourth letters of the consonant classes (*varga*). 39–40.
Now, those eight [consonants] ending in a long *visarga* are designated as *nāda*.
The two *guru* [syllables] are designated as *nāda*, and the two *anunāsika* [syllables] are likewise *laghu*. Both conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) and *visarga* are proclaimed to be *nāda*. 41.
Where five [consonants] are seen with a fifth [vowel] standing after them, one should apply the *nāsikya* there; when there is a single *mātrā*, there is no doubt.
At the end of a conjunction, however, there is a pause (*virāma*), and especially so in the case of a hiatus (*vivṛtti*).
In the *Saṃyuktāgra*, the unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) nasal is prescribed;

likewise, those unvoiced consonants and the vowels that stand as suffixes (*pratyaya*), as well as the five [nasalized vowels] at the end of a word (*padānta*) when conjoined, are indeed the five nasalized (*anunāsika*) sounds. 44.
In the opening, at the conclusion, and likewise in the middle of a half-verse, as well as in a word or when a quarter-verse is situated there, the *nāsikya* is prescribed;
the letter *ha*, when joined with *ra*, becomes the *nāda* eternally. 45–46.
Tread upon with two feet, yet never by *nāda*;
where there are two *sakāra*s at the beginning and end, and the letter *ha* is situated in the middle—both *nāda*s should be employed there. "O Agni, Lord of Vows" is the illustration. 47.
When an *anusvāra* occurs for both the letter *na* and the letter *ma*, one should know that it applies to both the short and long vowels in nasalized (*anunāsika*) syllables;
furthermore, semivowels (*antaḥstha*) are adjacent to the letters *na* and *ma*. 48–49.
The *nāsika* (nasal) should not be disregarded; therein the *nāda* (sound) is proclaimed.
When followed by a word ending in the *tavarga*, the *pavarga*, or a consonant, one should produce the *nāda* there; it is proclaimed that the final [consonant] is not [subject to this]. 50.
Wherever the letter *ha* is seen either before or after [another sound], there the *nāda* (resonance) certainly exists; of this there is never any doubt.
Likewise, wherever it occurs after the letter *na* or after the letter *ma*, [the same applies]. 51–52.
Wherever the letter *ha* is seen, there *nāda* will certainly be present; wherever the letters *na*, *ma*, and *u* are seen, unvoiced consonants (*aghoṣa*) follow them.
One should diligently produce *nāda* there, for the strength of the voiced sounds (*ghoṣa*) does not exist [there]. 53.
The single syllable of the letter *na* [is formed] from both vowels;
above that is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the unvoiced consonants (*aghoṣa*) stand before it.
The fifth [consonant] and the half-moon [are placed] between the two sibilant (*ūṣman*) vowels.
The example "nṛḥ pāhi" (protect the men) indeed serves to illustrate the aspirated sounds;
these twenty are the aspirates: g, jh, ḍh, dh, bh; ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m; y, r, l, v, h.
There are thirteen non-aspirates: k, c, ṭ, t, p; kh, ch, ṭh, th, ph; ś, ṣ, s.
That which is pronounced through both the mouth and the nose is called *anunāsika* (nasalized).
The two *ja*s, the *ma*, and the *ra* situated above them—one should know this as the bodiless *yama*; "sammārjmi" is the illustration. 57–58.
Even a piśāca roars in an empty house, yet it is not seen at all;

likewise, the vowels (varṇas) should be employed [with care], as illustrated by the example "upajjan. When the single syllable *va* occurs in the position of a particle (nipāta), [it functions as such].
That which is light in the *saṃhitā* becomes heavy at the time of the *pada* division.
(60) The letter *va* is said to be of three kinds: heavy, light, and very light.
It is heavy at the beginning [of a word], light in the middle, and very light at the end of a word. (61)
When the letter *va* is seen at the end of a word or in the middle of a word, it should be considered light;
indeed, it is even lighter elsewhere. When the word ending in *au* precedes and the letter *a* follows, [the *va* is light]. 62.
One should understand that "fire in fire" is an illustration of being very light [in articulation].
Just as a mother of children kisses them again and again out of affection, so too should the phonemes be employed; this is the illustration for the practitioner (*yuñjāna*). 63–64.
If a mare urinates while assuming whatever kind of posture she desires, the wise man should direct his face accordingly; this is the illustration of the *dundubhi* [breath].
If both [the *u*] are seen at the end of the letter *u* and at the letter *u* itself, [it is so].
One should understand that "dvirauṣṭhya" (the doubling of labials) is the illustration of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
That which occurs as a single sequence (*ekapadya*) is called "sakṛdauṣṭhya" (once-labial);
then follow "dvitribhiḥ" (twice or thrice), "catuṣka" (fourfold), and beyond that, "caturauṣṭhya" (four-labial). 66–67.
Just as two monkeys, engaged in a fight, run about with their mouths open, so should the phonemes be articulated; "like a peacock" (kikidīva) is the illustration.
Even a cock, though greedy for meat, utters two *ka* sounds.
Thus the syllables should be employed; "kukkuṭo 'si" is the illustration (69).
Again, there is a sentence of fourteen syllables, and again one of eleven syllables, and again a sentence of ten syllables, and after that one of eight syllables (70).
If one recites [the Veda] devoid of its characteristics or likewise without the ancillary texts (*vyañjana*),

the wise man makes that sound "siṃ" as an illustration, thinking, "You are a lioness. However, those who know the Vedas understand that he who recites the Veda without his hands [is likewise deficient].
But one devoid of the tallakṣaṇa is like food without condiments (72).
Thus, the fourfold statement and the illustration "Śrīśca te" [are examples]; a sentence consists of eight syllables and may have three or four feet (73).
The *gāyatrī* consists of seven syllables; "Agnir dūtaḥ" is the illustration.
Both [the next two] phrases consist of seven syllables, and then again there is one of nine syllables (74).
One should know that the phrase beginning with "yat puruṣeṇa" consists of eight syllables; this is the illustration.
That same three-verse hymn (*ṛc*), beginning with the eight-syllabled [mantra] in four quarters, should be recited;
at the end, the preceding verse should be properly concluded with the *svāhā* call for each individually.
That indeed is the correct characteristic, according to the doctrine of Pārāśara.
The Yājñavalkī, Vāsiṣṭhī, Kātyāyanī,
Pārāśarī, Gautamī, Māṇḍavyā, Amoghanandinī,
and Pāṇinīya Śikṣās are celebrated in all the Vedas and in all the Śāstras. (77)
In the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, the Mādhyandina recension is recorded there:
the first [mantra] consists of eleven syllables, the second has nine syllables,
the third should have eleven (the number of Rudras), and the fourth has eight (the number of treasures).
A sentence should consist of exactly four groups of forty syllables;
thus the phonemes are to be employed, as illustrated by the example "eṣa vastomā.
In a mantra where the letter *va* is seen between two short vowels at the beginning and end [of a word-group], [it is to be treated accordingly].

That [euphonic combination] is declared to be "hrasva" (short), as illustrated by the example *abhiyudhya*. Furthermore, that which follows the vowel *a* and is not used as long (*dīrgha*) should be understood as "abhividhi" (inclusive) in both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.

In the forests and in the intermediate space, he indeed beheld eight [worlds]; likewise, at the times of pronouncing names, it is the Guru alone who does so, without a doubt. (83) The preceding *kaṇḍikā* has been observed as being connected with those that follow.
That indeed is the mention of the name, never a conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Where the preceding [verse] is pierced by the subsequent *kaṇḍikā*, and where the word "cāpalāni" is seen, that should be known as the illustration of the *āccha* meter. 84–85.
Just as one burdened by a heavy load sighs, so should the phonemes (*varṇas*) be employed; this is the illustration regarding the Hotṛ priest saying "he shall sacrifice" (*hotā yakṣat*).
Two sentences have arisen here, consisting of nineteen syllables.
The *hotṛ* [verse] "mitrā pṛthivyā" consists of twenty-three syllables;
"haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" is known as having twelve syllables.
Thus, seventy-eight syllables have been proclaimed here.

These twelve sentences beginning with the letter *a* in number consist of seven [sentences]: the first and the fifth each have twelve syllables, while the subsequent sentence has six syllables; thus, another twelve are traditionally taught.
There is an eleven-syllable [pāda] and at the end a twelve-syllable one; thus the syllables are to be employed. Now, here is an illustration:
Prajāpati consists of three half-[pādas] and three full [pādas]. 91.
"punantu me" consists of four [verses], "vāyuḥ" follows with five,
then "anādhṛṣṭā" has five, and "edho'si" has four half-verses (92).
"saṃvatsaro'si" has four, and "dyauḥ śāntiḥ" consists of two half-verses.

In some cases one should utter "svāhā" separately, while in others one should cause it to be joined [to the mantra]. In some instances one should know it occurs at the beginning, and in others it is prescribed at the end; for example: "May the ancestors purify me," "Vāyu, the wind," and "For Prajāpati, you. 93–94.
At the time of the utterance of the mantra and at its conclusion, one should cast the oblation at the end of the word *svāhā*.
One should separate the portion of the mantra and pronounce the word *svāhā* separately for each.
The mantra may begin with *svāhā*, as in "Agni is the messenger" (*agnir dūtaḥ*) and likewise "the mind" (*manaḥ*).
At the beginning, in the middle, and again at the end, the visualization is "kāya svāhā" (96).

At the beginning of the letter *ma*, there is a sentence; the *ūrṇāmrada* is revealed. Manifesting from the mortal world, it begins with the letter *a* and ends with a vowel, being the first interval (97).

The number of sentiments (rasas) constitutes the sentence; then, repeatedly, there are four and five [syllables]. At the end of the pairs and the arrows [there are] seven, and at the very end fourteen.
By measure, the total number of phonemes and syllables is fifty-eight.
This very thing is to be understood; therefore, let there be no [other] statement.

99. "Thou art a spade. "O Agni, him today... "The measure of a thousand. "Agni is the deity. This is the head of Maravas above. "I thee for the horse. "The first of you two. "Between Mitra and Varuṇa."

The Hotṛ priest shall sacrifice to Agni with Svāhā! Svāhā to the sacrifice, to the soft-leafed sacrificial grass (barhis)! There is one syllable for the word and the sentence; there is no [extra] syllable in either half or in the couplets.
There is one syllable in the middle of the sentence, and two syllables each at the ends of the two halves.
Thus the phonemes are to be employed, as proclaimed according to worldly usage.
One should understand the case-endings either from a teacher or from the scriptures.
This is the determination of sentences through elision, augmentation, and modification;
these twelve are the sentences for the rite of pacification (śāntika). 101–102.
For the gods and the others, these twelve [syllables] exist by number;
"chāyā," "chidrā," and likewise "chandaḥ" [beginning with] the letter *cha* are counted as light. Whether short or long, the remaining [syllables] are established in pairs. (103)

According to the injunctions of the scriptures, one should recognize that a double syllable occurs when a *cha* follows a long vowel, and likewise when it follows a short vowel (104). Furthermore, O Giriśa, when a long vowel follows another long vowel, as in the case of *varmaṇā*, [the same rule applies] (105).

One should understand the duality of syllables through the illustration: the letter *va* is concealed by two *bha*s, the letter *cha* by two *ca*s, the letter *dha* by two *da*s, and the letter *tha* by two *ma*s. (106)
Of the *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, the *kha*-group, and the two *pa*-groups, there occurs doubling as well as the *yama* sound; this is certain, without doubt.
Furthermore, the labial [consonants] and the letter *v* are accompanied by the letter *m*. 107–108.

The conjunction of *taṃ* and *va* is extremely rare; likewise, the conjunction of *taṃ* and *vaś* is exceedingly difficult to find. (109) The wise have declared that one should not separate the *anusvāra*.
A bindu is established between the letter *va* and the letter *ya*.
Those remaining semivowels (*antasthā*), excluding the final bindu, are proclaimed to be like the horns of a young calf and like the pair of breasts of a maiden. (110–111)
That [sound] with the visarga is remembered as being like the eye of a black serpent;
for the limbs of the Veda exist like sparks of fire.
Indeed, due to impure recitation, they did not attain liberation.
Therefore, with every effort, a twice-born man should be one who recites the pure text;
otherwise, they go to the terrible Kumbhīpāka hell.
[The mantra consists of] seven syllables, four [syllables], and again eight syllables.
One should know that "ṛcaṃ vācam" is at the end, and there is a group of four;
the sentence consisting of eleven syllables is again followed by another group of four.
The examples are "trayodaśam" and "dvādaśam," as well as "yann me. (115)
In this context, the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis shall consist of three and a half [verses];
there are likewise four Praṇavas, of this there is no doubt.
At the beginning, there are the Ṛc, the Vāk, the three, and the quartet.
Thus has Pārāśara declared this authoritative teaching, which is equal to the Veda:
"The first [verse] consists of fourteen syllables, then three of twelve, then two of eleven, and finally one of ten.
In this manner the syllables are to be employed; "and Agni" is the illustrative example.
First the eight-syllable phrase, and thereafter the twelve-syllable one;
or having determined the two-footed [verse]: "Indra rules over the universe," just as the days [are three] and the others are likewise three for the sake of well-being. 119–120.
The last two are the "dwelling at the end" (antyāvasānā) and the "evil friend" (durmitrā); the remaining ones are proclaimed in pairs.
[The sequence is: four, five, two and a half, four, five, nine, nine;
again four, three, and again three, and so on repeatedly. 121.
One should know that the remaining half-verse pairs are the illustration of the Deity.
Having understood this, whoever recites it shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu.
There are three, three, and three, and then four. 122–123.
Six and a half, three, and two; five at the end of the last two;
and all the remaining *kaṇḍikās* are proclaimed to consist of two halves each.
(124) "No brahmin is dear to me, even if he is full of faith and fond of guests."
Thus it was spoken by Pārāśara out of a desire for the welfare of the brahmins, for the benefit of his disciples, and indeed for the sake of the next world:
"Svāhā! To the breaths, three; and likewise to the body hairs, three."
All the remaining *kaṇḍikās* are proclaimed as two *ardhas* each;
their *vākyas* are eight, seven, five, and twelve again,
then ten, one, and eighteen thereafter.
The ninth, the eighth, and then the seventh;
thus is the rule of the syllables correctly explained, along with the illustration from the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Vāyu becomes fivefold, and in each half there are two [syllables] in the golden [portion]. 128–129.
Of the mantra beginning with "Īśāvāsyam," two verses each are proclaimed as the remainder;
the sentence consisting of eighteen syllables is indeed for the Nākapṛṣṭha,
while this one of seventeen syllables should be designated as Vaiśvadeva.

A sentence of seventeen syllables followed by one of eighteen syllables—thus should the phonemes be employed; however, in the *supañca* meters, both [feet] consist of seven syllables, and after that, eight syllables.
131. Both [feet] consist of seven syllables, and after that, eight syllables.
One should understand the nine-syllable [mantra] as "ya-ar-m-i-ṣ-u-c-e-t-i"; this is the illustration.

Homages to each individual [syllable] are for the sake of the Great Soul Śaṅkara; they should occur at the beginning of the syllables and at the end of the syllables during the time of the recitation. 133–134.
By the constant recitation of the Namaka, the Camaka, and the Puruṣasūkta,
Mahādeva enters [the reciter] just as a householder enters his home.
Indeed, by means of the Rudrādhyāya with its proper intonation, through its ten sections (kaṇḍikās), [He is invoked].
Then one should utter the mantra at the end of the *ṛc*, consisting of sixteen syllables;
or again, a sentence of eighteen syllables with sixteen auspicious [syllables].
Thus the phonemes should be employed; this is specified as the "stone-born" (*aśman-nirjja*).

Wherever the words *pum̐ścalūm̐* and *pum̐ścalī* occur, they should be understood as having two dots (*daṅkṣṇavaḥ*); likewise, in the six instances [of the word *ardhacandra*], there are six half-moons. When the letter *cha* follows the letter *ma*, it is joined with an anusvāra.
One should recognize *tandra* as the meter; fire is the animal, which serves as the illustration.
(139) When a word ending in the letter *ta* is preceded by [the conditions] and the letter *śa* follows it, one should recognize that as *kṣaṇika*; "tat śakeyam" is the illustration. (140)
At the time of recitation, they should be short, but at the time of forming a sentence, they should be long;
thus should the phonemes be employed, as illustrated by the examples "nakṣatrebhyaḥ svāhā," "śarma ca sttha," and "stathopaprāgāt samudrasya. 141. And [the examples] "tvā" and "iti."
Even at the time of sentence formation, a circumflex (*svarita*) does not result in an acute (*udātta*);
for example, in *ehy ū ṣu ṛjīte abhi tvā gomad ū ṣuṇā satyā*, although it is a circumflex at the time of sentence formation, the hand is not raised upward. 142–143.
"You are the ocean born at once; you are indeed the first object of worship.

Thus, the two classes of consonants (sibilants and aspirates) should be employed by the Guru alone, without a doubt. (144) In some cases, when there is a conjunction with the semi-vowels (antastha), a stop (sparśa) is observed [to be substituted].
Then, being swallowed by the vowel *ṛ*, it is neither light nor lighter;
the syllable *ṛ* attains heaviness when joined with consonants (*harayaḥ*). This is an illustration of the rule: "By the reduction of the following [vowel] through the *ṛ*-sound. (145–146)
"Destroy the sacrificial rites, the enemies, the lords of the forest, and the enclosing-sticks"—
even a Brahmin who knows the four Vedas, as long as he does not find the Brahman,
wanders in this worthless and difficult-to-cross cycle of worldly existence. 147.
Having studied the four Vedas and all the various scriptures in many ways,
he who does not know Brahman is a fool, like one who is deceitful in his recitation;
but having known [Brahman], one attains union with Brahman— of this there is no doubt.
Just as a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows only the weight but not the sandalwood itself,
so too, O Brahmins, those who are filled with the Smṛtis and Vedas but devoid of wisdom carry them like a donkey.
Eating, sleeping, fear, and sexual intercourse— these are common to humans and animals alike.

For knowledge is their superior distinction; those devoid of knowledge are equal to beasts. (151) Bound by urine and excrement in the morning, by hunger and thirst at midday, and by desire at night, living beings are held captive, being under its sway. (152)
Thousands and hundreds of millions of *nāda*s and *bindu*s, along with rays accompanied by the vital breath, proceed toward that place where the Veda is free from affliction;
just as the milk of cows of many colors becomes of a single color. 153.

Just as milk is to a cow, so is knowledge to the possessor of signs. There are two words for liberation: "not mine" and "mine. By destroying the notion of "this is mine," one destroys enemies without wasting away. 154–155.
The five *arañjanās* are half [in duration], and the *ardhamātrās* are also [half];
Pūṣan, Mitra, and Vasu are proclaimed as the *añjanāśvas*.
Pūṣan, Mitra, and the five Vasus are proclaimed as the *anurañjanās*.

These five consonants—vakṣya, yakṣya, kakṣya, bhakṣya, and māṇā—are each composed of one and a half morae (ardhamātrā) and serve as embellishments; these letters are known to be palatals (tālavya), while those that follow are remembered as cerebrals (mūrdhanya). 157–158.
He who recites [this] after knowing it thus shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu.
"No brahmin is dear to me; one who recites purely is very dear to me.
Thus it was spoken by Pārāśara out of a desire for the welfare of the brahmins.
For the benefit of disciples and for the welfare of the next world,
thus ends the Pārāśarī Śikṣā.
